turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Many runners drink coffee before a race. Does caffeine really improve performance?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes, it's one of the best-studied legal ergogenic aids. That means substances that help you perform better. Research shows it can improve endurance performance by a few percent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The main explanation involves adenosine receptors in the brain. During the day, and during exercise, a chemical called adenosine builds up and makes you feel tired. Caffeine blocks the receptors, so adenosine has less effect.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. Studies show that caffeine lowers perceived exertion. That's how hard the exercise feels. The same pace feels a little easier, so you can push harder or longer.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A common range in research is about three to six milligrams per kilogram of body weight, often taken around an hour before the start. For many people, even lower amounts can work. A strong cup of coffee might have around one hundred milligrams.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Definitely. Too much caffeine can cause shaky hands, a fast heartbeat and stomach problems. It can also ruin your sleep the night after the race. And people respond very differently. So test it carefully during training, not for the first time on race day.
